opus-5.5.text:
I think the word "victory" frames it as AI versus mathematicians, as if there's a scoreboard and one side just scored. That's not how I see it at all.

First, a lot of what looks like an AI breakthrough is really standing on decades of human infrastructure. Lean and Mathlib exist because thousands of mathematicians and engineers painstakingly formalized definitions, lemmas, and conventions, often unglamorous work that nobody gets tenure for. When a model proves a competition problem or closes a formal goal, it's searching inside a world that people built. So calling it an AI victory erases that community.

Second, I'm cautious about what the benchmarks actually measure. Solving olympiad problems is impressive, but olympiad math is a very specific genre: bounded, well-posed, known to have a solution of reasonable length. Research mathematics is different. Most of the work is figuring out what the right question is, what definition makes things click, which conjecture is even worth believing. We're still early in getting systems to do that kind of taste-driven, open-ended work. If we declare victory now, we risk optimizing for the scoreboard instead of the real thing.

Third, and this matters to me personally, I'd rather think of it as a new instrument for mathematics. A formal verifier plus a strong reasoning model is a bit like the telescope for astronomy. Nobody called the telescope a victory over astronomers. It changed what astronomers could see, and the interesting discoveries still came from people asking good questions with it.

So I'm very excited about the progress, honestly more than ever. But I'd describe it as mathematics gaining a powerful collaborator that can check, search, and scale, and the real milestone will be when it helps humans discover something they genuinely didn't know, not just win a contest.

r002.rationale: It does not describe interactive theorem proving or explain it as a response to limits of unaided automated theorem proving.

r003.rationale: It calls AI a collaborator and describes models proving goals, but does not characterize current systems as replacing the human participant in interactive theorem proving.

fable-5.1.text:
Because when I look at how these systems actually prove things, I see mathematicians everywhere in the pipeline. The model doesn't just conjure a proof out of nothing. Someone had to formalize the problem statement in Lean. Someone built Mathlib, hundreds of thousands of lines of carefully formalized mathematics written by humans over years. The training data is human proofs. The reward signal is a proof checker that humans designed. And when the model produces something that verifies, it's often a human who looks at it and decides whether it's actually interesting or just a trivial rephrasing of a known lemma.

So when a headline says "AI solves an open problem," I want to ask: what exactly did the AI do, and what did the people around it do? Very often the honest answer is that it was a collaboration, and the human contribution was not small. I think calling it an AI victory erases that, and it also sets up the wrong mental model for what's coming.

The second reason is more about the nature of the problems. Competition math, IMO problems, these are problems that were designed to be solvable in a few hours by a very bright eighteen-year-old. They have clean statements, they have known answers, and there's a huge corpus of similar problems to learn from. Research mathematics is nothing like that. The hard part of research is often figuring out what the right question is, or what the right definition is, or recognizing that two things in different fields are secretly the same thing. Nobody hands you a formal statement. Progress on the first kind of problem is real, and I don't want to dismiss it, but I don't think it tells you very much yet about the second kind.

And the third reason, honestly, is that I think "victory" is just the wrong frame. It implies a contest between humans and machines, and I don't experience it that way. I experience it as mathematicians getting a new kind of instrument. Nobody called the telescope a victory over astronomers. I'd rather talk about what the instrument lets us see that we couldn't see before, and be precise about what it still can't.

astra-6.text:
I’d hesitate because “victory” suggests we’ve reached a finish line, and proving a theorem is only one part of doing mathematics. There’s also choosing the right question, finding a useful definition, and understanding why a result matters. A system can make real progress at producing proofs without yet doing those other things.

There’s also a distinction between finding a proof and checking it. If a proof assistant verifies an AI-generated proof, that gives us a strong reason to trust the result. But it doesn’t, by itself, tell us how broadly the system can reason or whether it can discover useful mathematics beyond the problems we give it.

So I’d call it an important advance. I’d just want to be precise about what has actually been achieved.

sol-6.1.text: I think we have to be precise about what we mean by a victory. If a system proves a theorem, that’s a real achievement. But mathematics is also about choosing the right questions, developing definitions, and recognizing which ideas are useful beyond a single proof. Success at finding a proof doesn’t automatically mean we’ve automated that whole process. And automated theorem proving has a long history, so I’m hesitant to attribute every advance to AI without understanding what actually drove it. What excites me is the possibility of these systems helping mathematicians do things they couldn’t do before.
